clue.text: No-one at Cannes that could be common

parts.note: taken as written
un is French for one, and Cannes is in France

explanation.surface: Nobody in the French resort is ordinary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No-one' looks like one word meaning nobody but splits in two; 'common' is grammar, not ordinariness.
explanation.definitionFit: A common noun is a grammatical category, so a noun is something that could be common.

clue.text: Swordsman regularly on call visiting ladies?

indicators.note: a visitor goes inside a place, so these letters are put inside the other word

parts.note: dames are ladies, titled women

indicators.note: taking letters at regular intervals, here every other letter of the two words

explanation.surface: A fencer is often on the phone to some women.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' takes OCL from 'on call', which goes into DAMES. Damocles is not a fighter: a sword hung by a hair over his head, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek legend a sword dangled above Damocles at a banquet, so he is a man defined by a sword, playfully a swordsman.

clue.text: Fast runner's beaten hare

indicators.note: something beaten is knocked out of shape, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A speedy athlete has defeated the hare.
explanation.definitionFit: The rhea is a large flightless South American bird that runs very quickly.

clue.text: Cast racing round at first — that's natural

indicators.note: tells us the round letter is placed at the front of the rest

parts.note: O is round in shape

indicators.note: to cast metal is to shape it anew, so these letters are reshaped

explanation.surface: A racing team is set out with the first lap — all quite normal.
explanation.definitionFit: Organic produce is grown naturally, without artificial chemicals.

clue.text: Copper arresting unknown country fireman?

indicators.note: a policeman arresting someone holds them, so these letters go inside

parts.note: PC, police constable, is a copper
Y is an algebraic unknown
Romania is a European country

explanation.surface: A policeman detains a foreign firefighter of uncertain origin.
explanation.walkthrough: A fireman normally puts fires out; the question mark says this one starts them.
explanation.definitionFit: An arsonist with a compulsion to start blazes could jokingly be called a fire-man.

clue.text: Dog active, see, with tail docked

indicators.note: something active is moving about, so these letters are stirred around
docking a tail cuts off the end, so the last letter of the word is removed

explanation.surface: A lively dog, look, has had its tail cut short.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tail docked' takes H off 'with', and 'active' rearranges SEE + WIT.
explanation.definitionFit: A Westie is a West Highland white terrier, a breed of dog.

clue.text: Put up with Hungary's president

parts.note: H is the international vehicle code for Hungary
Ike was the nickname of US President Eisenhower

explanation.surface: Someone tolerates the Hungarian head of state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put up with' reads as tolerate, but 'with' is only a link: 'Put up' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To hike prices is to raise them.

clue.text: Letter idiot attempted to hide

indicators.note: the word is concealed inside the clue text that follows

explanation.surface: A fool tried to conceal a letter he'd written.
explanation.definitionFit: Iota is the ninth character of the Greek alphabet.

clue.text: Hound dangerous when one's going for run

indicators.note: one letter goes and another takes its place

parts.note: hairy is slang for dangerous
I is the Roman numeral one
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: A hunting dog is risky when someone sets off running.
explanation.definitionFit: To hound and to harry both mean to pester persistently.

clue.text: Lamb in trouble — ewe finally brought back

indicators.note: bringing something back reverses its direction, so these letters run backwards

parts.note: to ail is to trouble

indicators.note: picks the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: A lamb in distress has its mother returned to it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brought back' reverses AIL + E. Lamb is the essayist Charles Lamb, not a young sheep.
explanation.definitionFit: Elia was the pen name Charles Lamb used for his essays.

clue.text: Land a record catch nearly on return

indicators.note: a return goes back the way it came, so these letters are read backwards

parts.note: a log is a record

indicators.note: nearly means the word lacks its last letter

parts.note: to nab is to catch

explanation.surface: Landing a record-breaking haul on the way home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nearly' cuts NAB to NA, and 'on return' reverses A + LOG + NA.
explanation.definitionFit: Angola is a country in southern Africa, and a country is a land.

clue.text: Supporter of pelota's turning nasty

indicators.note: a person turning nasty changes their nature, so these letters change order

explanation.surface: A fan of the Basque ball game becomes aggressive.
explanation.walkthrough: Pelota is a Basque court game. 'turning nasty' rearranges PELOTAS.
explanation.definitionFit: An apostle is a committed advocate of a cause, a supporter.

clue.text: Picked up burn in seaside resort

indicators.note: what the ear picks up is a sound, so the word is said aloud

parts.note: a burn, Scottish for a stream, is a rill

explanation.surface: A sunburn caught at the beach.
explanation.walkthrough: Burn here is a stream, not sunburn. Rhyl is a seaside town in north Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhyl is a Welsh coastal holiday town, a resort by the sea.

clue.text: Beautiful woman's demand for attention — say you are engaged!

indicators.note: being engaged means being taken in, so these letters are held inside

parts.note: Hoi! is a shout to get someone's attention

indicators.note: say signals that the words are spoken, and sounded out they are two letters

parts.note: you are, spoken, sounds like the letters U and R

explanation.surface: A lovely woman calls out to announce she is to be married.
explanation.walkthrough: Engaged suggests a proposal, but here it signals insertion.
explanation.definitionFit: In Islamic tradition a houri is a beautiful maiden of paradise; the word is used for any lovely woman.

clue.text: Fool! One very involved with environment's beginning to gush (when going by this?)

indicators.note: being involved means caught up inside, so these letters go within

parts.note: a prat is a fool
I is the Roman numeral one

indicators.note: picks the first letter of the word

parts.note: to jet is to gush out

explanation.surface: A rant at an idiot who cares about the planet yet flies privately.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracketed question makes the whole clue point to the answer: someone fussing about the environment while travelling by this.
explanation.definitionFit: A privately owned plane is a way of going, and environmentalists criticise travel by one.

clue.text: Before mixing rum and rice wine — top quality

parts.note: pre- is a prefix meaning before

indicators.note: mixing drinks combines and stirs them, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Ahead of a cocktail of rum and sake comes the best stuff.
explanation.definitionFit: Premier cru is a French classification for the finest vineyards, so it labels top-rank wine.

clue.text: Kick out old footballer who can't finish

parts.note: ex- means former, old

indicators.note: someone unable to finish stops short, so the last letter is removed

parts.note: Pelé was a famous Brazilian footballer

explanation.surface: Sack a veteran footballer who can't score.
explanation.definitionFit: To expel someone is to throw them out, a synonym of kick out.

clue.text: Commonwealth citizen is French too (and English)

parts.note: aussi is French for too, also

explanation.surface: A member of the Commonwealth is also French, and English as well.
explanation.definitionFit: Aussie is informal for an Australian, and Australia is a Commonwealth country.

clue.text: I drag back one tree

indicators.note: back means the word is turned round and read backwards

parts.note: to drag is to pull
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Someone hauls a single tree backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The illupi is an Indian tree, also called the mahua, whose seeds give a butter-like fat.

clue.text: Posh boy Henry grabbed — I owned up

indicators.note: something grabbed is held tight, so these letters are taken inside

parts.note: a lad is a boy
H is the symbol for the henry, the unit of inductance

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the word is written upwards, backwards

parts.note: had means owned

explanation.surface: A smart young man seized Henry, and I confessed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'owned up' looks like confessed, but 'up' reverses HAD.
explanation.definitionFit: Lah-di-dah describes affectedly genteel, pretentious manners, which is posh.

clue.text: Post result of this interruption to journey

parts.note: the answer's two words read as a recipe: the first word, its letters shuffled as the second word orders, gives the clue's word post

explanation.surface: Mail is what comes from this break in a trip.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a reverse clue: the answer is wordplay, and the clue word is what it makes.
explanation.definitionFit: A stop-off is a brief halt partway through a trip, which breaks the journey.

clue.text: 'Facile!' as was written about current member with agenda

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so these letters go round the rest

parts.note: sic is Latin, used to mark text as originally written
I is the physics symbol for electric current
MP, Member of Parliament
an agenda is a list of items

explanation.surface: An easy jibe, quoted verbatim, about a sitting MP with a programme.
explanation.definitionFit: A facile argument is superficial and oversimplified, which is what simplistic means.

clue.text: Jokes about a couple of heartless hoaxes

indicators.note: about means going round, so the first word encloses the other

parts.note: puns are jokes

indicators.note: the heart, the middle letter, is removed

parts.note: a couple is two

explanation.surface: Jokes concerning a pair of cruel pranks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heartless' removes the middle letter; 'about' puts the jokes round what remains. 'Jokes' looks like the definition, but it is the hoaxes.
explanation.definitionFit: A put-on is a deception or trick played on someone, so put-ons are hoaxes.

clue.text: Lethal force keeps order locally

indicators.note: the phrase keeps the answer inside it, a run across the two words

explanation.surface: Deadly force maintains law and order in the neighbourhood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'order locally' is not law and order: it is what you ask for at the local, the British word for your nearby pub.
explanation.definitionFit: A half, meaning half a pint of beer, is a typical drink to ask for at the pub.

clue.text: Time for Philip to protect supporter of mine

indicators.note: protecting means surrounding, so these letters go inside

parts.note: Pip is a short form of Philip
pro means for, in favour of

explanation.surface: Time for Philip to look after someone backing me.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Time for Philip' looks like a substitution, but 'for' supplies PRO.
explanation.definitionFit: A pit prop is a timber or steel post holding up the roof of a mine tunnel.

clue.text: Power cut — glad to have survived that!

parts.note: to hew is to cut

explanation.surface: A blackout, and relief at getting through it.
explanation.definitionFit: Phew is an exclamation of relief after a narrow escape.

clue.text: Worth engaging new singer?

indicators.note: engaging means taking in, so the letter is put inside the word

parts.note: worth is price, value

explanation.surface: Is it worthwhile hiring a fresh vocalist?
explanation.definitionFit: Prince was the stage name of the American pop star; the question mark warns that a prince is usually royalty.

clue.text: Pose dressed for not much money

indicators.note: dressing something arranges it differently, so these letters change order

explanation.surface: A model clothed for a small fee.
explanation.definitionFit: The peso is a currency unit of several Latin American countries, worth little in some.

clue.text: Smart hotel guarded by top soldier initially

indicators.note: the guards stand round it, so the letter is put inside

parts.note: the top soldier is the Commander-in-Chief, whose initials are CIC
H is hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A stylish hotel protected by the general.
explanation.definitionFit: Chic describes elegant, stylish dress or looks, which is smart.

clue.text: Foot not party leader for a very long time

indicators.note: not means without, so the letter is taken away

parts.note: a paeon is a metrical foot of four syllables in poetry

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its opening letter, here of party

explanation.surface: Michael Foot was not a party leader for long.
explanation.walkthrough: Foot is a unit of verse here; Michael Foot led the UK Labour Party briefly in the early 1980s.
explanation.definitionFit: An aeon is an immensely long age, an indefinitely vast period.

clue.text: Female in prison returned to cause divisions

indicators.note: in means the letter is placed inside the other part
something returned goes back, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: stir is slang for prison

explanation.surface: A woman sent back to jail causes splits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returned' turns STIR into RITS, which takes F inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Rifts are breaks in a relationship, splits or divisions.

clue.text: One song rejected for another

parts.note: a means one

indicators.note: rejected means thrown back, so the word is reversed

parts.note: an air is a song or tune

explanation.surface: One song is turned down in favour of a different one.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is 'another' song: an aria is a song, like the air.
explanation.definitionFit: An aria is a solo song in an opera, so it is one more song alongside the first.
